findings.description: PickleSerializer.loads() uses pickle.loads on data - by-design deserialization API, already deprecated for security reasons
findings.reasoning: The sink is inside Django's explicitly opt-in PickleSerializer helper class. Django's own documentation warns that the cache/session/serializer backends which use pickle must only be given trusted data ("If you are using pickle, make sure the data is trusted"). In this version the class even emits RemovedInDjango50Warning, i.e. upstream has already deprecated and removed this API precisely because of the security risk. The data passed to loads() originates from the application developer choosing the pickle serializer, not from request input, so there is no attacker-controlled flow.

evidence.code_context: PickleSerializer.dumps/loads around line 20-45 of django/core/serializers/base.py, with deprecation warning at __init__
evidence.dataflow_analysis: No path from an HTTP request / user input to loads(); callers are developer-selected session/cache serializer settings. Documented prerequisite: data must be trusted.
evidence.notes: Library-intentional API with explicit warning; not a vulnerability of this code, mitigation is documented and enforced by deprecation.

Reading it back only deserializes data this application previously stored. findings.description: FileBasedCache.get() pickle.loads on cache file contents
findings.reasoning: The file path is derived from md5(key) inside the configured cache directory (self._dir), so there is no path traversal, and the content was written by this same Django process via _write_content() using pickle.dumps. Deserializing the local cache directory is Django's documented behavior (CACHES with the file backend require a directory writable only by the app user). An attacker who can write into the cache directory already has code-execution-equivalent filesystem access.

evidence.code_context: _key_to_file() = os.path.join(self._dir, md5(key).hexdigest() + suffix); _write_content writes pickle.dumps(expiry) + zlib(pickle.dumps(value))
evidence.dataflow_analysis: No request data influences the unpickled bytes; requires local filesystem write to the cache dir.
evidence.notes: Trusted local cache boundary, documented in Django cache docs; not remotely exploitable.

findings.description: FileBasedCache.touch() pickle.loads on cached value read back from cache file
findings.reasoning: Same trusted-local-cache reasoning as get(): the bytes are re-read from a file this process wrote (pickle.dumps) inside the app-owned cache directory, and the file name is an md5 of the cache key. No attacker-controlled input reaches the pickle.loads call.

evidence.code_context: touch() re-reads the value to rewrite it with a new expiry
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Round-trip of the process's own serialized value; no external source.
evidence.notes: Trusted filesystem cache boundary.

findings.description: FileBasedCache._is_expired() unconditionally unpickles the expiry header of a cache file
findings.reasoning: _is_expired() reads only the header written by _write_content() (pickle.dumps(expiry, ...)) from files inside the app-owned cache directory. Exploitation requires the ability to place a malicious file in that directory, which already implies filesystem write access equal to the app user, i.e. a pre-existing compromise. Not reachable from untrusted request input.

evidence.code_context: Expiry header written with pickle.dumps(expiry, self.pickle_protocol) in _write_content()
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Files enumerated only from self._dir via glob1 with cache_suffix; no user-controlled path or content.
evidence.notes: Documented trusted-cache assumption.

findings.description: eval() on argparse-selected subcommand name in a developer maintenance script
findings.code_snippet:
parser.add_argument("cmd", nargs=1, choices=RUNABLE_SCRIPTS)
    ...
    options = parser.parse_args()

    eval(options.cmd[0])(options.resources, options.languages)
findings.reasoning: The eval() argument is `options.cmd[0]`, which is constrained by argparse `choices=RUNABLE_SCRIPTS` where RUNABLE_SCRIPTS = ("update_catalogs", "lang_stats", "fetch"). argparse rejects any value not in that tuple, so the eval can only ever resolve one of three fixed local function names. In addition, this file is a standalone i18n maintenance script under scripts/ (not part of the shipped django package or any request-handling path), executed manually by a Django committer on their own machine. There is no attacker-controlled input path and no privilege boundary crossed, making this a false positive.

evidence.code_context:
RUNABLE_SCRIPTS = ("update_catalogs", "lang_stats", "fetch")
parser.add_argument("cmd", nargs=1, choices=RUNABLE_SCRIPTS)
options = parser.parse_args()
eval(options.cmd[0])(options.resources, options.languages)
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source: sys.argv -> argparse parse_args. argparse enforces choices=RUNABLE_SCRIPTS, raising SystemExit for any other value, so the sink only receives one of 3 hardcoded identifiers. No propagation of arbitrary strings to eval().
evidence.notes: Developer-only script in scripts/, not installed with the django package, not reachable from web requests.

findings.description: yaml.load in the PyYAML serializer uses SafeLoader, which cannot instantiate arbitrary objects
findings.code_snippet:
try:
        yield from PythonDeserializer(yaml.load(stream, Loader=SafeLoader), **options)
findings.reasoning: The yaml.load call explicitly passes `Loader=SafeLoader` (aliased to `yaml.CSafeLoader` when the libyaml C extension is available, otherwise `yaml.SafeLoader`). SafeLoader only constructs standard YAML types (dict/list/str/int/etc.) and raises ConstructorError for arbitrary python/object tags, so the classic `!!python/object/apply:os.system` RCE payload does not work. The resulting data is a plain list/dict that is then fed to PythonDeserializer, which builds model instances from a whitelisted set of fields rather than unpickling. There is no unsafe deserialization here; the query matched the `yaml.load` name pattern only.

evidence.code_context:
try:
    from yaml import CSafeDumper as SafeDumper
    from yaml import CSafeLoader as SafeLoader
except ImportError:
    from yaml import SafeDumper, SafeLoader
...
yield from PythonDeserializer(yaml.load(stream, Loader=SafeLoader), **options)
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source: user-supplied serialized stream -> yaml.load(..., Loader=SafeLoader) -> plain python primitives -> PythonDeserializer (field-by-field model construction). SafeLoader blocks arbitrary tag construction, so no object instantiation sink is reachable.
evidence.notes: SafeLoader is the documented-safe loader; unsafe usage would require Loader=yaml.Loader / FullLoader / UnsafeLoader. This is the pattern Django has used since the CVE-2011-4103/2013 era fix.

findings.description: eval() of an interactive prompt answer in the migration questioner (local operator input, documented behavior)
findings.reasoning: This eval() is part of Django's documented interactive `makemigrations` flow: when a non-nullable field is added, the developer is prompted at the terminal to type a one-off Python literal default. The input comes from `input()` on stdin of the operator running the command, not from any HTTP request, template, or untrusted data source. The globals dict is empty and locals are limited to datetime/timezone. Anyone able to type into this prompt already has shell access as the developer and could simply run code directly, so no privilege boundary is crossed. Known-and-intended behavior, not a vulnerability in Django itself.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source: stdin via input() in an interactive management command run locally by the developer. Sink: eval with empty globals. No remote/untrusted source, no request context.
evidence.notes: Documented in Django docs under 'Providing defaults' for migrations; the prompt is explicitly asking the user to write Python code.

findings.description: pickle.loads fallback in the Redis cache client's default serializer (trusted-cache assumption)
findings.reasoning: This is the legacy default serializer of Django's Redis cache backend. The data being unpickled comes from the configured Redis server, which is a trusted infrastructure component: an attacker who can write arbitrary values into the Django Redis cache instance already controls a backend store that holds session data, cached permissions, and pickled values for every other cache backend as well (db.py, filebased.py, locmem.py all use pickle identically). Django's documented security model treats cache/DB/queue backends as trusted, and the setting CACHE_SERIALIZER (JSON) is the recommended mitigation. There is no path for untrusted request data to reach this sink without first compromising the Redis server, so this is an architectural/design consideration rather than an exploitable vulnerability in Django. Note Redis cache became the default in Django 4.0 and Django explicitly documents "cache backends use pickle; only use trusted cache servers".

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Data flows from the Redis server (network store configured via CACHES) into pickle.loads. Attacker must already be able to inject arbitrary values into that Redis instance (i.e., already control a trusted backend), at which point the trust boundary is already broken.
evidence.notes: JSONSerializer is available and documented as the hardened option; pickle-based caching is a known, documented design property of Django (and all Python cache backends).

findings.description: exec() of $PYTHONSTARTUP / ~/.pythonrc.py content in the shell management command (intended feature)
findings.code_snippet:
with open(pythonrc) as handle:
                    pythonrc_code = handle.read()
                # Match the behavior of the cpython shell where an error in
                # PYTHONSTARTUP prints an exception and continues.
                try:
                    exec(compile(pythonrc_code, pythonrc, "exec"), imported_objects)
findings.reasoning: This mirrors CPython's own interactive-interpreter startup behavior: if $PYTHONSTARTUP or ~/.pythonrc.py exists, its contents are executed before the shell starts. The file is supplied by the local user via their own environment/home directory; executing it is the entire purpose of the feature and grants no capability the user did not already have (they can run python directly). Mitigations include --no-startup and the fact that the file must exist and be readable. No remote or untrusted input reaches this sink, so it is a false positive.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source: local filesystem/env var controlled by the invoking user. Sink: exec. No untrusted/remote source; --no-startup disables the behavior entirely.
evidence.notes: Documented in Django's 'shell' command docs; matches CPython -i startup semantics.

findings.description: exec() of the -c/--command argument of `manage.py shell` (explicit documented code execution)
findings.reasoning: The `-c/--command` option of `manage.py shell` exists specifically to execute a Python snippet supplied by the developer on the command line. The "attacker" would have to already have local shell access as the account running manage.py, so exec'ing the string grants zero additional privilege. There is no web request, no untrusted data source, and this is documented behavior. Not a vulnerability.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source: argv from the local operator. Sink: exec. Requires prior local access with the same privileges as the process.
evidence.notes: Equivalent to `python -c '...'`; intentional feature of the shell command.

findings.description: XML deserialization appears to parse untrusted XML with pulldom, but the parser is explicitly hardened against DTDs and external entities (no XXE)
findings.code_snippet: self.event_stream = pulldom.parse(self.stream, self._make_parser())
findings.reasoning: The flagged call `pulldom.parse(self.stream, self._make_parser())` passes a parser built by `_make_parser()`, which returns `DefusedExpatParser()`. `DefusedExpatParser.__init__` disables `feature_external_ges` and `feature_external_pes`, and `reset()` additionally installs handlers that raise `DTDForbidden`, `EntitiesForbidden` and `ExternalReferenceForbidden` for DOCTYPE declarations, entity declarations and external entity references. Therefore external entity expansion (XXE) and XML bombs are blocked; this is the exact defusedxml mitigation for CWE-611.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: XML input (stream_or_string) -> pulldom.parse(stream, DefusedExpatParser()) -> external entities / DTDs rejected by hardened handlers. No unsanitized path to an entity-expanding parser found.
evidence.notes: grep for DefusedExpatParser shows it is defined at line 408 of the same module and used exclusively by _make_parser().

findings.description: Flagged 'filesystem operation' at ImageField.to_python is Pillow opening an uploaded file object, not a caller-controlled filesystem path
findings.code_snippet: image = Image.open(file)
findings.reasoning: The reported line is `image = Image.open(file)` inside `ImageField.to_python()`. The `file` object is either `BytesIO(data.read())` (in-memory bytes of the uploaded file), `BytesIO(data["content"])`, or `data.temporary_file_path()` — a path generated by Django's upload handlers (TemporaryUploadedFile), never a user-supplied path string. The web-supplied value only becomes file *content*, so no path traversal is possible here. The dataflow path shown by CodeQL merely tracks an uploaded value through ArrayField/GeometryField `.clean()` into this method; there is no attacker-controlled path component reaching a filesystem API. The `open()` destination used later for saving uploads is handled by `FileSystemStorage`, which applies `validate_file_name`/`get_available_name` protections.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: CodeQL flow: django/contrib/postgres/forms/array.py:33-34 (ArrayField.to_python split) -> django/forms/fields.py:193/198 (Field.clean) -> 696 (FileField.clean) -> 715 -> 720 Image.open(file). The tainted value is file content/upload object, not a path string. django/contrib/gis/forms/fields.py:67-73 path is analogous (GeometryField).
evidence.notes: No os.path / open() call on a user-supplied filename at this location; Pillow is fed an in-memory buffer or a server-generated temp path.

findings.description: TarArchive.extract writes members through BaseArchive.target_filename(), which validates the resolved path against the extraction root (zip-slip mitigated), with a residual startswith-prefix weakness
findings.code_snippet:
with Archive(path) as archive:
        archive.extract(to_path)
findings.reasoning: The flagged call is only the thin public wrapper `extract(path, to_path)` that delegates to `Archive.extract()` -> `TarArchive.extract()`/`ZipArchive.extract()`. Those implementations do not blindly extract members; every member name goes through `BaseArchive.target_filename()`, which resolves `os.path.abspath(os.path.join(target_path, name))` and raises `SuspiciousOperation` unless the absolute result starts with the abspath of `to_path`. This blocks ordinary `../` and absolute-path zip-slip payloads. The tainted input here is a local path chosen by a developer/CLI user (management command or library call), not remote HTTP input. Residual concern (reported separately) is that `startswith()` is a prefix test rather than a component test; however it is not sufficient to mark this wrapper itself as an exploitable path traversal.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: extract(path,to_path) -> Archive.extract -> TarArchive.extract/ZipArchive.extract -> target_filename() validation -> open(filename,'wb'). Source is a local filesystem path provided by the caller, not a remote request parameter.
evidence.notes: tests/utils_tests/test_archive.py:94 asserts the SuspiciousOperation message, confirming the protection is intentional and tested.

findings.description: Archive.extract() delegating method - extraction is guarded by target_filename() validation; no unguarded extraction occurs
findings.code_snippet: self._archive.extract(to_path)
findings.reasoning: Line 92 is the delegation inside `Archive.extract(self, to_path)`. Both concrete implementations (`TarArchive.extract`, `ZipArchive.extract`) route each member name through `BaseArchive.target_filename()` which abspaths the joined path and rejects results that escape `to_path`, and the archive source paths come from local callers (library API / management command), not from HTTP input. Hence the reported sink is a protected delegation, not an exploitable traversal.

evidence.dataflow_analysis: Archive.extract -> TarArchive.extract -> target_filename(to_path, member.name) -> SuspiciousOperation on escape; ZipArchive.extract identical.
evidence.notes: Residual prefix-based startswith weakness in target_filename noted separately.

findings.description: Archive extraction of a template archive in the `startapp`/`startproject` management command (django/core/management/templates.py) — flagged as Zip Slip, but extraction is protected by BaseArchive.target_filename's abspath containment check
findings.reasoning: Line 255 is inside `TemplateCommand.handle()` where `handle_template()` is invoked to obtain the template directory (which, for archives, comes from `self.extract(...)` → `django.utils.archive.extract`). The actual extraction sink is in `django/utils/archive.py`, where `BaseArchive.target_filename()` computes `filename = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(target_path, name))` and raises `SuspiciousOperation("Archive contains invalid path: ...")` when `filename` does not start with `os.path.abspath(to_path)`. That check blocks `../` escapes and absolute member names for both TarArchive and ZipArchive. Additionally, this code path is only reachable from a local operator running `django-admin startapp/startproject --template=<path-or-url>`; the archive is chosen by the operator themselves, not by a remote untrusted request. Note: `str.startswith` string prefix comparison (rather than commonpath) is theoretically weaker for sibling dirs sharing a prefix, but combined with `os.path.abspath` on both sides and the operator-controlled CLI input, this is not an exploitable vulnerability here. Not a true positive.

evidence.code_context:
target_filename():
    target_path = os.path.abspath(to_path)
    filename = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(target_path, name))
    if not filename.startswith(target_path):
        raise SuspiciousOperation("Archive contains invalid path: '%s'" % name)

evidence.notes: Only reachable via local management command with operator-supplied template; extraction library enforces path containment. Test suite validates 'Archive contains invalid path' behavior (tests/utils_tests/test_archive.py:94).

findings.description: Archive extraction in `TemplateCommand.extract()` (django/core/management/templates.py) flagged as unsafe archive extraction (Zip Slip); the underlying archive utility enforces a path-containment check on every member
findings.reasoning: `TemplateCommand.extract()` (line ~379) calls `archive.extract(filename, tempdir)`. That helper delegates to `Archive.extract()` → `TarArchive.extract()` / `ZipArchive.extract()`, both of which compute each output path via `BaseArchive.target_filename()`: `filename = os.path.abspath(os.path.join(os.path.abspath(to_path), name))` and raise `SuspiciousOperation` unless `filename.startswith(os.path.abspath(to_path))`. Leading `/` and `\\` are stripped in `split_leading_dir`, and tar symlinks are read via `extractfile()` and written as regular files (so no symlink-based escape). Extraction target is a fresh `tempfile.mkdtemp()`. The `filename` (archive to extract) comes from the local operator via `django-admin startapp/startproject --template=`, i.e. the same privilege level as running arbitrary code. Hence this is a defense-in-depth alert rather than an exploitable path traversal.

findings.description: Header value set from trusted Django settings (SECURE_CROSS_ORIGIN_OPENER_POLICY) is not attacker-controllable; ResponseHeaders.__setitem__ also rejects CR/LF via BadHeaderError, so no HTTP response splitting is possible.
findings.reasoning:
The flagged sink in SecurityMiddleware.process_response sets the Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy header using self.cross_origin_opener_policy, which is assigned in __init__ directly from settings.SECURE_CROSS_ORIGIN_OPENER_POLICY (django/conf/global_settings.py: SECURE_CROSS_ORIGIN_OPENER_POLICY = "same-origin"). This value originates from the server's own configuration file, not from any HTTP request data, so there is no untrusted source and no exploitable dataflow (CWE-113 requires attacker-controlled input reaching the header).

Additionally, defense in depth exists: all header writes go through ResponseHeaders.__setitem__ (django/http/response.py:82-91), which calls _convert_to_charset and explicitly raises BadHeaderError if "\r" or "\n" is present in either the header name or value. So even a misconfigured/CRLF-containing setting value could not result in a split response — it would raise an exception instead of emitting an injected header.

The Django check framework (django/core/checks/security/base.py, security.E024) further validates that the setting is one of the allowed CROSS_ORIGIN_OPENER_POLICY_VALUES. Same reasoning applies to the other headers written in this middleware (Strict-Transport-Security from SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS booleans, Referrer-Policy from SECURE_REFERRER_POLICY). This is a benign, settings-only header write, i.e. a false positive for a header-injection query.

evidence.code_context:
django/middleware/security.py:19 -> self.cross_origin_opener_policy = settings.SECURE_CROSS_ORIGIN_OPENER_POLICY
security.py:62-65 -> response.setdefault("Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy", self.cross_origin_opener_policy)
django/conf/global_settings.py:674 -> SECURE_CROSS_ORIGIN_OPENER_POLICY = "same-origin"
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Source is settings (server-side configuration), not a request object. No path from HTTP request data (request.META, headers, query params, bodies) to the header value; therefore no attacker-controlled flow to the sink.
evidence.notes: Sanitizer/mitigation confirmed in django/http/response.py:50-90 - ResponseHeaders._convert_to_charset raises BadHeaderError when '\n' or '\r' appear in a header name or value; ResponseHeaders.__setitem__ applies this to every header write. Check framework security.E024 also restricts SECURE_CROSS_ORIGIN_OPENER_POLICY to an allowlist of values.
